lean_implies_source.reasoning: The Lean proposition proves Jensen only after assuming both X and φ ∘ X are Integrable. It therefore does not entail the source's stated claim for every random variable, because it yields no conclusion when either added premise fails. The common case with integrable X but nonintegrable φ ∘ X, where E[φ(X)] may be +∞ and extended-value Jensen remains meaningful, is expressly outside the Lean theorem.

source_implies_lean.reasoning: The source's universally stated Jensen inequality specializes to the subclass in which X and φ ∘ X are integrable. On that subclass D001 and D029 give the same finite real Lebesgue expectations, D005 gives the same global real convexity, and the displayed inequality is identical, so the source claim entails the Lean conditional proposition.

findings.source_evidence: The selected sentence states Jensen for any random variable X and convex φ : ℝ → ℝ, without an explicit integrability premise.
findings.lean_evidence: The target has separate premises hX : Integrable X μ and hφX : Integrable (φ ∘ X) μ.
findings.impact: The target omits all source-stated cases failing either premise. Added hypotheses make the formal theorem less applicable and therefore weaker for this audit; they do not make it faithful-stronger.

findings.source_evidence: The source does not say E[φ(X)] must be finite and supplies no exclusion of an infinite right-hand expectation.
findings.lean_evidence: hφX requires finite absolute integrability, so expectation μ (φ ∘ X) is a finite real value.
findings.impact: A standard Jensen case with integrable X but E[φ(X)]=+∞ can satisfy the source inequality in an extended-value reading but is unavailable in Lean, confirming Lean⇒source is no while source⇒Lean is yes.

findings.source_evidence: The source calls X any random variable even though φ(E X) needs a meaningful finite E X, and it does not specify an extended-expectation convention.
findings.lean_evidence: hX resolves this ambiguity by ensuring E X is a finite real number; hφX additionally forces the right side finite.
findings.impact: Some integrability restriction is a reasonable formal well-definedness choice, but the source does not select both Lean premises. This does not erase the literal applicability gap, especially the unnecessary finiteness restriction on φ ∘ X.

rationale: The target faithfully represents the Jensen formula, real-valued binders, probability-space setting, expectation-as-integral convention, global convexity, composition order, and inequality direction. Its decisive discrepancy is domain: requiring Integrable X and Integrable (φ ∘ X) turns the source's unrestricted 'any random variable' statement into a conditional finite-integral theorem. Under the audit protocol, such extra hypotheses are reduced applicability. Hence the source result implies the Lean specialization, but the Lean specialization does not imply the source's full stated result, giving not-faithful-weaker and accepted=false.
